where: Exam traps, trap 1 (reversing the current-source arrow)
problem: The sentence contradicts itself. A voltage source drives current through the outside circuit out of its + terminal and back to its − terminal. The arrow inside the equivalent current source points from − to +, which is the opposite spatial direction to the current in the outside circuit. Telling a student the arrow must 'point the same way the voltage source drove current through the outside circuit' invites exactly the reversal this trap is warning about.
fix: The arrow inside the current source points from − to + (toward the source's + terminal). Current then leaves that + terminal, flows through the outside circuit, and returns to the − terminal. The + terminal of the equivalent voltage source is the terminal the arrow points to.

where: Section 1, bullet on pointing the arrow
problem: 'Point the arrow inside the current source from − to +; that is the direction it pushes current through the outside circuit' reads as if the internal arrow and the external current are the same direction. They are not; the external current leaves the + terminal and runs back to −.
fix: Point the arrow inside the current source from − to +, toward the terminal that acts as +. Current leaves that terminal into the outside circuit and returns to −.

where: Quiz Q6 (why convert a star to a delta in a bridge)
problem: The stated reason is weak and can mislead. The standard bridge simplification is delta-to-star: the delta is replaced by a star, which breaks the loop and gives series-parallel branches. Converting a star to a delta usually adds a mesh and rarely helps reduction, so 'this is why we convert' teaches the less useful direction.
fix: The delta of 12 Ω replaces the star of 4 Ω. In most bridges the useful direction is the opposite one, delta to star, because it removes the loop and leaves plain series-parallel branches; a star-to-delta is used only when the new delta sides land in parallel with existing branches.
